summary: Provides education and guidance for IETF participants on complying with antitrust laws and reducing antitrust risk in connection with IETF activities.

plainLanguage.summary: When competing companies meet to make shared rules, they must be careful not to unfairly gang up against others. This is a guide to staying within the law.

questions: what antitrust rules apply to ietf participants
what topics should i avoid at ietf meetings
how do i report antitrust concerns at ietf
subtitle: Guidelines for competing companies collaborating safely at the IETF.

tldr.problem: When competitor companies meet to create shared standards, they risk violating antitrust law if they discuss pricing, market strategy or other anticompetitive topics.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF has established policies that prevent anticompetitive behavior by requiring participants to act as individuals using best judgment for the Internet, and by providing clear guidance on what topics to avoid.
tldr.outcome: Participants are educated on antitrust law, IETF's safeguards are reinforced, and reporting mechanisms exist for concerns.

today: RFC 9680 is an active informational RFC that provides current guidance. It is not a standard and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Antitrust Matters in Standards Work
sections.content:
The IETF brings together engineers from competing companies who collaborate on Internet standards. This creates a natural tension: antitrust laws (also called competition laws) prohibit agreements that unfairly restrict competition, yet standards work requires cooperation among competitors. The RFC educates participants on how to comply with antitrust law while continuing to work together.

Antitrust laws protect consumers and businesses from anticompetitive behavior. The core goal is to ensure fair and open competition in the marketplace, allowing better prices, quality and choice. The IETF has a dual responsibility: first, to prevent the IETF organization itself from creating liability through anticompetitive conduct; second, to avoid being a forum where participants engage in anticompetitive behavior that harms the IETF's reputation.
sections.plainLanguage: When many companies work together to make rules everyone follows, the government makes sure they don't secretly cheat and unfairly prevent other companies from competing. The IETF needs to follow these rules.

sections.title: IETF Compliance Mechanisms
sections.content:
The IETF already has strong antitrust safeguards built into its structure. Participants engage as individuals, not as company representatives, and are expected to use their best engineering judgment for the whole Internet. The IETF's core policies ensure open and fair participation:

  • The Internet Standards Process (BCP 9) defines fair, open procedures with appeals mechanisms.
  • Working Group Guidelines (BCP 25) require open participation and thorough consideration of alternatives.
  • Intellectual Property policies (BCP 78 and 79) ensure terms are fair and benefit the Internet community.
  • Conflict of Interest policies are in place for IESG, IAB and the IETF LLC.

Compliance with these existing policies naturally mitigates antitrust risk. Following them ensures that standards development remains collaborative without crossing into anticompetitive territory.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF has built-in rules that keep things fair: people speak for themselves, not their companies; everyone gets heard; the smartest answers win; and no one can hoard the results unfairly.

sections.title: Topics to Avoid
sections.content:
While most IETF discussions are safe, some topics are dangerous and should not be discussed in a standards setting where competitors are present. Participants should be aware of and avoid:

  • Discussion of product pricing or profit margins among potential competitors
  • Details of business relationships between vendors and customers
  • Supply chain information about specific companies
  • Market opportunities for specific companies
  • Employee compensation or benefits at competing employers

These topics create serious antitrust risk. Even if a discussion of these topics would not necessarily violate antitrust law in isolation, the presence of competitors and the collaborative context of standards work makes them particularly dangerous. The safest approach is to avoid them altogether in IETF forums.

It is important to remember that antitrust law extends beyond these specific topics. Any behavior that amounts to an agreement to restrain marketplace competition or that facilitates monopolization can raise antitrust concerns. Participants are personally responsible for ensuring their conduct does not violate antitrust law.
sections.plainLanguage: Don't talk about how much things cost, who buys from who, how many workers people hire, or which markets are good to enter. If you talk about any of these with your competitors, you could get in trouble.

sections.title: Obtaining Legal Advice and Reporting
sections.content:
The IETF does not provide legal advice to participants. Participants should obtain their own independent legal counsel when they have questions about whether a topic or discussion presents antitrust risk. This is the responsibility of each participant and their organization.

If a participant becomes aware of potential antitrust issues in the context of IETF activities, they can escalate them in two ways:

  • Contact IETF legal counsel at legal@ietf.org
  • Use the IETF LLC whistleblower service

It is important to note that the IETF will assess reports for their impact on the IETF itself. Participants who are directly affected by an antitrust issue remain responsible for obtaining their own legal advice and pursuing their own remedies.
sections.plainLanguage: If you're not sure if something is allowed, ask a lawyer at your company or for your company. If you see something wrong happening, tell the IETF's lawyers, but they can't give you legal advice.
